content: Onchocerciasis, also known as river blindness, is a neglected tropical disease caused by the parasitic worm Onchocerca volvulus. The disease is transmitted through repeated bites by black flies of the genus Simulium. These flies thrive and breed near fast-flowing streams and rivers, which is why the disease is commonly referred to as river blindness. The infection can lead to blindness, as well as skin diseases such as subcutaneous nodules and severe itching. Globally, onchocerciasis is the second leading infectious cause of blindness, following trachoma. Dr. Rodolfo Robles Valverde's research on patients with river blindness in Guatemala was instrumental in identifying Onchocerca volvulus as the causative agent. His work also provided critical insights into the life cycle and transmission of the parasite. Onchocerciasis can be classified into different types based on the specific cutaneous lesions observed in affected individuals. The disease spreads from person to person through the bite of an infected black fly. When a black fly bites an individual with onchocerciasis, microscopic worm larvae, known as microfilariae, are ingested by the fly. These larvae develop within the fly over approximately two weeks, reaching an infectious stage. When the infected black fly bites another person, it deposits the larvae onto the skin, where they penetrate and infect the individual. The worms reproduce exclusively in humans but require part of their development to occur within the black fly. The intensity of infection in humans is directly related to the number of infectious bites sustained. The causative agent, Onchocerca volvulus, is a nematode primarily found in Africa. Like most filarial nematodes, O. volvulus has a symbiotic relationship with the bacterium Wolbachia. The absence of Wolbachia disrupts or halts the larval development of the parasite. Patients with onchocerciasis may present with symptoms such as skin rashes, eye disease, and subcutaneous swelling. It is important to differentiate onchocerciasis from other diseases with similar clinical manifestations. Onchocercal infections are predominantly found in tropical climates, with approximately 99% of cases occurring in Africa. The parasite is also present in limited areas of the Americas and Yemen in the Middle East. Those at highest risk include individuals living in endemic areas, as well as long-term travelers, missionaries, and Peace Corps volunteers who are exposed to black fly bites for extended periods (typically more than three months). The disease is most intensely transmitted in remote rural African agricultural villages located near rapidly flowing streams. The natural history of onchocerciasis includes complications such as inflammation of the optic nerve, which can lead to vision loss, particularly peripheral vision, and eventually blindness. Infected individuals may be asymptomatic, but those with symptoms typically exhibit one or more of the following: itchy skin rashes, eye disease, and subcutaneous nodules. The most severe manifestation involves ocular lesions that can result in visual impairment and blindness. The gold standard for diagnosing onchocerciasis is the skin snip biopsy. This procedure involves removing a small piece of skin (approximately 3 mm in diameter) using a needle and scalpel or a sclerocorneal biopsy punch. Antibody tests are also available to aid in diagnosis, though many are limited to research settings. The treatment of choice for onchocerciasis is ivermectin. This medication has been shown to reduce the occurrence of blindness and alleviate the severity of skin symptoms. Doxycycline, which targets the Wolbachia bacteria, can also be used to disrupt the development of O. volvulus macrofilariae and embryogenesis. However, doxycycline does not kill microfilariae, so ivermectin is often required to achieve a more rapid reduction in symptoms. There are currently no vaccines or medications available to prevent infection with O. volvulus. Primary prevention efforts focus on personal protection against black fly bites. These measures include the use of insect repellents containing N,N-Diethyl-meta-toluamide (DEET) on exposed skin, wearing long sleeves and pants during the day when black flies are active, and using permethrin-treated clothing.
